claim: The spindle generates force to segregate chromosomes at cell division.
source: The spindle generates force to segregate chromosomes at cell division.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in cell biology supported by extensive prior research.

claim: In mammalian cells, kinetochore-fibers connect chromosomes to the spindle.
source: In mammalian cells, kinetochore-fibers connect chromosomes to the spindle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian spindle structure.

claim: Microneedle manipulation can exert local forces on the spindle with spatiotemporal control.
source: Here, we adapt microneedle manipulation to exert local forces on the spindle with spatiotemporal control.
evidence: The manuscript describes the development and application of this technique with experimental demonstrations.

claim: Pulling on kinetochore-fibers reveals the preservation of local architecture in the spindle-center over seconds.
source: Pulling on kinetochore-fibers reveals the preservation of local architecture in the spindle-center over seconds.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from microneedle manipulation experiments.

claim: Sister, but not neighbor, kinetochore-fibers remain tightly coupled, restricting chromosome stretching.
source: Sister, but not neighbor, kinetochore-fibers remain tightly coupled, restricting chromosome stretching.
evidence: This finding is supported by measurements of inter-kinetochore distance and deformation propagation shown in Figure 2.

claim: Pulled kinetochore-fibers pivot around poles but not chromosomes, retaining their orientation within 3 μm of chromosomes.
source: Further, pulled kinetochore-fibers pivot around poles but not chromosomes, retaining their orientation within 3 μm of chromosomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by curvature analysis in Figure 3 showing negative curvature near chromosomes but not poles.

claim: Local reinforcement near chromosomes has a 20 s lifetime.
source: This local reinforcement has a 20 s lifetime, and requires the microtubule crosslinker PRC1.
evidence: This is measured directly in manipulate-and-hold experiments shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: Local reinforcement near chromosomes requires the microtubule crosslinker PRC1.
source: This local reinforcement has a 20 s lifetime, and requires the microtubule crosslinker PRC1.
evidence: This is demonstrated by PRC1 RNAi experiments in Figure 4 showing loss of negative curvature upon PRC1 depletion.

claim: Mechanical force helps build the spindle.
source: Mechanical force helps build the spindle, stabilize chromosome attachments (Nicklas and Koch, 1969), and ultimately move chromosomes (Inoué and Salmon, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mechanical force helps stabilize chromosome attachments.
source: Mechanical force helps build the spindle, stabilize chromosome attachments (Nicklas and Koch, 1969), and ultimately move chromosomes (Inoué and Salmon, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nicklas and Koch, 1969.

claim: Mechanical force helps move chromosomes.
source: Mechanical force helps build the spindle, stabilize chromosome attachments (Nicklas and Koch, 1969), and ultimately move chromosomes (Inoué and Salmon, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Inoué and Salmon, 1995.

claim: The mammalian spindle must generate and respond to force while maintaining a mechanically robust structure that can persist for about an hour.
source: To perform its function, the mammalian spindle must generate and respond to force while maintaining a mechanically robust structure that can persist for about an hour.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mitotic timescales.

claim: The spindle's microtubules turn over on the order of seconds and minutes.
source: Yet, to remodel itself during mitosis, the spindle must also be dynamic, with its microtubules turning over on the order of seconds and minutes (Gorbsky and Borisy, 1989; Saxton et al., 1984; Zhai et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on microtubule dynamics.

claim: A k-fiber is a bundle of 15–25 kinetochore-bound microtubules.
source: A key structural element of the mammalian spindle is the kinetochore-fiber (k-fiber), a bundle of 15–25 kinetochore-bound microtubules (kMTs) (McEwen et al., 1998) of which many reach the spindle pole (McDonald et al., 1992; Rieder, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citation to McEwen et al., 1998.

claim: Many kinetochore-bound microtubules in a k-fiber reach the spindle pole.
source: A key structural element of the mammalian spindle is the kinetochore-fiber (k-fiber), a bundle of 15–25 kinetochore-bound microtubules (kMTs) (McEwen et al., 1998) of which many reach the spindle pole (McDonald et al., 1992; Rieder, 1981).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McDonald et al., 1992 and Rieder, 1981.

claim: K-fibers generate force to move chromosomes.
source: K-fibers generate force to move chromosomes (Grishchuk et al., 2005; Koshland et al., 1988) and provide connections to opposite spindle poles.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: K-fibers make contacts along their length with a dense network of non-kinetochore microtubules.
source: K-fibers make contacts along their length with a dense network of non-kinetochore microtubules (non-kMTs) (Mastronarde et al., 1993; McDonald et al., 1992), likely through both motor and non-motor microtubule binding proteins (Elting et al., 2017; Kajtez et al., 2016; Vladimirou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to electron microscopy studies.

claim: K-fiber contacts with non-kMTs are likely mediated through both motor and non-motor microtubule binding proteins.
source: K-fibers make contacts along their length with a dense network of non-kinetochore microtubules (non-kMTs) (Mastronarde et al., 1993; McDonald et al., 1992), likely through both motor and non-motor microtubule binding proteins (Elting et al., 2017; Kajtez et al., 2016; Vladimirou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on inference from cited studies about microtubule binding proteins.

claim: The non-kMT network bridges sister k-fibers together.
source: We know that the non-kMT network bridges sister k-fibers together (Kajtez et al., 2016; Mastronarde et al., 1993; Tolić, 2018; Witt et al., 1981), and that it can locally anchor k-fibers and bear load in the spindle's longitudinal (pole-pole) axis (Elting et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: The non-kMT network can locally anchor k-fibers and bear load in the spindle's longitudinal axis.
source: We know that the non-kMT network bridges sister k-fibers together (Kajtez et al., 2016; Mastronarde et al., 1993; Tolić, 2018; Witt et al., 1981), and that it can locally anchor k-fibers and bear load in the spindle's longitudinal (pole-pole) axis (Elting et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Elting et al., 2017.

claim: The microneedle deformed the membrane locally, rather than globally pressing the membrane against the whole spindle.
source: We found that the microneedle deformed the membrane locally, rather than globally pressing the membrane against the whole spindle (Figure 1A–B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by membrane imaging data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: The overall cell height did not change upon manipulation.
source: Consistent with local deformation, the overall cell height did not change upon manipulation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The membrane appeared intact since the membrane contoured the microneedle during manipulation.
source: The membrane appeared intact since the membrane contoured the microneedle during manipulation (Figure 1B) and the cell impermeable dye propidium iodide did not enter the cell during and after manipulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Nicklas et al., 1982).
evidence: This is demonstrated by membrane imaging in Figure 1B.

claim: The cell impermeable dye propidium iodide did not enter the cell during and after manipulation.
source: The membrane appeared intact since the membrane contoured the microneedle during manipulation (Figure 1B) and the cell impermeable dye propidium iodide did not enter the cell during and after manipulation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Nicklas et al., 1982).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and cited as a method from Nicklas et al., 1982.

claim: The spindle returned to its original structure upon microneedle removal.
source: We imaged the spindle before, during and after the pull (Figure 1G, Figure 1—video 1) and found that the spindle returned to its original structure upon microneedle removal (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H comparing pre- and post-manipulation spindle structure.

claim: The spindle typically entered anaphase within 15 min of microneedle removal.
source: The spindle typically entered anaphase within 15 min of microneedle removal (Figure 1G, Figure 1—video 1), consistent with cell health.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1G and video, indicating cells remain viable after manipulation.

claim: The deformed k-fiber bent and deformations in the same spindle-half were only detectable within the first 5 μm from the microneedle.
source: The deformed k-fiber bent and deformations in the same spindle-half were only detectable within the first 5 μm from the microneedle (exponential decay constant = 0.44 μm−1 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A)), suggesting weak mechanical coupling between neighboring k-fibers (Elting et al., 2017; Vladimirou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is measured from strain maps and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The spatial decay of deformation suggests weak mechanical coupling between neighboring k-fibers.
source: The deformed k-fiber bent and deformations in the same spindle-half were only detectable within the first 5 μm from the microneedle (exponential decay constant = 0.44 μm−1 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A)), suggesting weak mechanical coupling between neighboring k-fibers (Elting et al., 2017; Vladimirou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the spatial decay data and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Increasing crosslinking with FCPT led to a more gradual spatial decay of deformation.
source: As a control, increasing crosslinking with a Kinesin-5 rigor drug (FCPT, n = 4 cells, Groen et al., 2008) led to a more gradual spatial decay of deformation (exponential decay constant = 0.25 μm−1 (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B)), with deformations propagating further through the spindle-half.
evidence: This is measured experimentally with FCPT treatment and shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Crosslinking strength tunes anchorage within the spindle and thereby modulates its material properties.
source: This is consistent with the idea that crosslinking strength tunes anchorage within the spindle and thereby modulates its material properties (Shimamoto et al., 2011; Takagi et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the FCPT experiment and supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Force propagation is dampened between neighboring k-fibers, which may effectively mechanically isolate them.
source: Together, these findings suggest that force propagation is dampened between neighboring k-fibers, which may effectively mechanically isolate them (Matos et al., 2009) and promote their independent functions.
evidence: This is inferred from the deformation data and supported by citation.

claim: Pulling on the k-fiber over 12 s did not lead to an increase in inter-kinetochore distance.
source: Surprisingly, pulling on the k-fiber over this short timescale did not lead to an increase in inter-kinetochore distance (distance between sister k-fiber plus-ends, Figure 2E,F).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Chromosomes relax and then stretch after k-fiber ablation near plus-ends over a similar timescale.
source: Yet, we know that chromosomes relax and then stretch after k-fiber ablation near plus-ends over a similar timescale (Elting et al., 2014; Sikirzhytski et al., 2014), indicating that they are elastic on the timescale of these manipulations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior ablation studies.

claim: The spindle shortened by 0.5 ± 0.1 μm in response to the manipulation.
source: Instead, the spindle shortened by 0.5 ± 0.1 μm in response to the manipulation (Figure 2E,G; Gatlin et al., 2010; Itabashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 2G, with citations to similar observations.

claim: A structure other than the chromosome couples sister k-fibers across spindle halves on the seconds timescale.
source: This suggests that a structure other than the chromosome couples sister k-fibers across spindle halves on the seconds timescale.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that inter-kinetochore distance doesn't increase despite pulling.

claim: The sister k-fiber moved in towards the pole-pole axis by 5.8 ± 0.9° upon pulling.
source: Consistent with this idea, the sister k-fiber, opposite the k-fiber being pulled, moved in towards the pole-pole axis by 5.8 ± 0.9° upon pulling (Figure 2E,H), preserving the angle between sister k-fibers (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The spindle maintains local architecture around chromosomes against transient forces, instead adjusting its global architecture.
source: Together, this reveals that the spindle maintains local architecture around chromosomes against transient forces, instead adjusting its global architecture, and that sister k-fibers are tightly crosslinked to each other on the seconds timescale at metaphase.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined observations of inter-kinetochore distance, pole-pole distance, and sister k-fiber angle measurements.

claim: Sister k-fibers are tightly crosslinked to each other on the seconds timescale at metaphase.
source: Together, this reveals that the spindle maintains local architecture around chromosomes against transient forces, instead adjusting its global architecture, and that sister k-fibers are tightly crosslinked to each other on the seconds timescale at metaphase.
evidence: This is inferred from the coordinated movement of sister k-fibers during manipulation.

claim: In 4 out of 7 cells manipulated over 12 s, a region of negative curvature was observed near the chromosome.
source: In the k-fibers manipulated over 12 s, we observed high positive curvature at the position of the microneedle and, unexpectedly, a region of negative curvature near the chromosome (n = 4/7 cells) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is measured from curvature analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The configuration with both positive and negative curvature is more energetically costly than a single bent region.
source: This configuration, more energetically costly than a single bent region, indicates that k-fibers are unable to pivot near their plus-ends, which is well suited to promote their biorientation.
evidence: This is based on physical principles of beam bending.

claim: K-fibers are unable to pivot near their plus-ends.
source: This configuration, more energetically costly than a single bent region, indicates that k-fibers are unable to pivot near their plus-ends, which is well suited to promote their biorientation.
evidence: This is inferred from the negative curvature observation.

claim: Negative curvature near chromosomes was observed in 74% of spindles manipulated for 60 s.
source: We observed negative curvature near the chromosome in 74% (n = 17/23) of the spindles, and near the pole in just 17% (n = 4/23) of the spindles (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is measured from curvature analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Negative curvature near poles was observed in 17% of spindles manipulated for 60 s.
source: We observed negative curvature near the chromosome in 74% (n = 17/23) of the spindles, and near the pole in just 17% (n = 4/23) of the spindles (Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is measured from curvature analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: K-fibers can easily pivot around poles.
source: This indicates that k-fibers can easily pivot around poles, as observed in insect cells (Begg and Ellis, 1979), but cannot do so around chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the low frequency of negative curvature near poles and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: K-fibers cannot pivot around chromosomes.
source: This indicates that k-fibers can easily pivot around poles, as observed in insect cells (Begg and Ellis, 1979), but cannot do so around chromosomes.
evidence: This is inferred from the high frequency of negative curvature near chromosomes.

claim: Manipulating the outer k-fiber often exposed non-kMTs in contact with the k-fiber.
source: Often, manipulating the outer k-fiber exposed non-kMTs in contact with the k-fiber (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1); this revealed connections observed in electron microscopy (McDonald et al., 1992; Nicklas et al., 1982), that are harder to see with light microscopy.
evidence: This is observed in manipulation experiments shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Non-kMT connections observed close to the region of negative curvature may contribute to reinforcing k-fibers in the spindle center.
source: These non-kMT connections, observed close to the region of negative curvature (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), may contribute to reinforcing k-fibers in the spindle center.
evidence: This is speculated based on the spatial correlation between non-kMT contacts and negative curvature.

claim: Negative curvature was always observed between 1 and 3 μm from the chromosome regardless of where the k-fiber was pulled.
source: Negative curvature was not correlated with microneedle position (Figure 3F), and was always observed between 1 and 3 μm from the chromosome regardless of where we pulled (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 3G.

claim: A specialized structure in the spindle center laterally reinforces k-fibers near chromosomes.
source: Instead, it strongly supports a model whereby a specialized structure in the spindle center laterally reinforces k-fibers near chromosomes (Model 2).
evidence: This is inferred from the consistent position of negative curvature near chromosomes regardless of pull location.

claim: The negative curvature near chromosomes lasted for 18.8 ± 2.6 s before it was no longer detectable.
source: The negative curvature near chromosomes lasted for 18.8 ± 2.6 s before it was no longer detectable, likely reflecting the lifetime of the underlying connections (Figure 3H–I, Figure 3—video 2).
evidence: This is measured in manipulate-and-hold experiments shown in Figure 3H-I.

claim: There is short-lived, non-uniform reinforcement of the k-fiber near chromosomes.
source: Together, these findings indicate the presence of short-lived, non-uniform reinforcement of the k-fiber near chromosomes that is stable enough to preserve spindle structure over short timescales, but sufficiently dynamic to allow spindle remodeling over long timescales.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the spatial localization and temporal lifetime measurements.

claim: PRC1 enrichment spanned a region of 6.9 ± 0.3 μm in the spindle center.
source: We found that PRC1 enrichment spanned a region of 6.9 ± 0.3 μm (n = 6 cells) in the spindle center (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is measured from immunofluorescence images shown in Figure 4B.

claim: PRC1 localization maps well to the expected location of a specialized crosslinker spanning the inter-kinetochore region and the region of mechanical reinforcement near chromosomes.
source: This maps well to the expected location of a specialized crosslinker, spanning the inter-kinetochore region (~2 μm), and the region of mechanical reinforcement near chromosomes (1–3 μm along each sister k-fiber).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing PRC1 localization to the measured reinforcement region.

claim: PRC1 depletion by RNAi resulted in a decrease in inter-kinetochore distance from 2.35 ± 0.04 μm in WT cells to 1.86 ± 0.09 μm in PRC1 RNAi cells.
source: Using immunofluorescence, we observed a decrease in the inter-kinetochore distance (from 2.35 ± 0.04 μm in WT cells to 1.86 ± 0.09 μm in PRC1 RNAi cells) (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A), similar to human cells (Polak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is measured from immunofluorescence and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: 91% of PRC1 RNAi spindles lacked a detectable k-fiber negative curvature near chromosomes upon pulling.
source: When subjecting PRC1 RNAi spindles to the same manipulation assay (deformed by 2.6 ± 0.1 μm over 66 ± 6 s (n = 12 cells)) as WT spindles (Figure 3), we found that 91% of the spindles lacked a detectable k-fiber negative curvature near chromosomes upon pulling (Figure 4D–E, Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is measured from curvature analysis in PRC1 RNAi cells shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: 76% of deformed k-fibers in WT cells showed negative curvature near chromosomes compared to only 8% in PRC1 RNAi cells.
source: In order to directly compare the WT and PRC1 RNAi datasets, we only looked at curvature profiles in which the distribution of microneedle positions overlapped: 76% (n = 13/17) of deformed k-fibers in WT cells showed negative curvature near chromosomes compared to only 8% (n = 1/12) of deformed k-fibers in PRC1 RNAi cells (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4F.

claim: PRC1 laterally reinforces k-fibers near chromosomes, and enables them to resist pivoting under force.
source: Thus, PRC1 laterally reinforces k-fibers near chromosomes, and enables them to resist pivoting under force.
evidence: This is concluded from the loss of negative curvature in PRC1 RNAi cells.

claim: In PRC1 RNAi spindles, the inter-kinetochore distance increased by 0.7 ± 0.1 μm upon manipulation, compared to 0.1 ± 0.1 μm in WT spindles.
source: In PRC1 RNAi spindles, the inter-kinetochore distance increased by 0.7 ± 0.1 μm upon manipulation, compared to 0.1 ± 0.1 μm in WT spindles (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4H.

claim: PRC1-mediated crosslinking resists both compressive and extensile forces.
source: This suggests that PRC1-mediated crosslinking not only resists compressive forces (Kajtez et al., 2016) but also extensile forces.
evidence: This is inferred from the increased inter-kinetochore distance in PRC1 RNAi upon pulling, with citation to prior work on compressive forces.

claim: Upon pulling, the sister k-fiber opposite the deformed k-fiber moved in towards the pole-pole axis by 4.5 ± 1.4° in PRC1 RNAi cells, less than in WT cells where it moved by 10.6 ± 1.2°.
source: Furthermore, upon pulling, the sister k-fiber opposite the deformed k-fiber moved in towards the pole-pole axis by 4.5 ± 1.4°, less than in WT cells where it moved by 10.6 ± 1.2° (Figure 4G,I).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4I.

claim: The angle between the sister k-fibers' chromosome-proximal regions was less well-preserved after manipulation in PRC1 RNAi than in WT.
source: Finally, the angle between the sister k-fibers' chromosome-proximal regions was less well-preserved after manipulation than in WT (Figure 4G,J).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4J.

claim: PRC1 promotes tight coupling between sister k-fibers, ensuring they behave as a single mechanical unit and maintain biorientation.
source: These findings suggest that PRC1 promotes tight coupling between sister k-fibers, ensuring they behave as a single mechanical unit and maintain biorientation.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined observations of inter-kinetochore distance, sister k-fiber angle, and angle between sister k-fibers in PRC1 RNAi.

claim: Microtubule intensity remains similar upon PRC1 depletion.
source: While we do not know if PRC1 acts directly or indirectly to locally reinforce k-fibers, we find that microtubule intensity remains similar upon PRC1 depletion (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that it is unlikely to act simply by changing microtubule density in the spindle.
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B.

claim: PRC1 provides the specialized, short-lived structural reinforcement in the spindle center near chromosomes.
source: Together, our findings indicate that PRC1 provides the specialized, short-lived structural reinforcement in the spindle center near chromosomes.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined PRC1 localization and RNAi manipulation experiments.

claim: PRC1 is a passive molecular force generator that preferentially binds anti-parallel microtubules.
source: Here, we find a spatially and temporally well-defined role for PRC1, a passive molecular force generator that preferentially binds anti-parallel microtubules (Mollinari et al., 2002) and can maintain and reinforce microtubule overlaps in vitro (Bieling et al., 2010; Braun et al., 2011; Wijeratne and Subramanian, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on PRC1 properties.

claim: PRC1 can maintain and reinforce microtubule overlaps in vitro.
source: Here, we find a spatially and temporally well-defined role for PRC1, a passive molecular force generator that preferentially binds anti-parallel microtubules (Mollinari et al., 2002) and can maintain and reinforce microtubule overlaps in vitro (Bieling et al., 2010; Braun et al., 2011; Wijeratne and Subramanian, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to in vitro studies.

claim: PRC1 can help promote chromosome stretch.
source: In the longitudinal axis, PRC1 can help promote chromosome stretch, which has been proposed to maintain tension and biorientation of sister-kinetochore pairs (Polak et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work.

claim: PRC1 can help limit chromosome stretch, thereby mechanically buffering chromosomes from transient forces.
source: We find that PRC1 can also help limit chromosome stretch (Figure 4H), thereby mechanically buffering chromosomes from transient forces.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the increased inter-kinetochore distance in PRC1 RNAi upon manipulation shown in Figure 4H.

claim: PRC1's microtubule binding is phosphoregulated during mitosis.
source: PRC1's microtubule binding is phosphoregulated during mitosis (Mollinari et al., 2002; Zhu and Jiang, 2005; Zhu et al., 2006), and as such these frictional forces may be regulated as the spindle's mechanical functions change.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on PRC1 regulation.

claim: PRC1 restricts pivoting of k-fibers around chromosomes, even under external force, thereby promoting biorientation between sister k-fibers.
source: In the lateral axis, we find that PRC1 restricts pivoting of k-fibers around chromosomes (Figure 4D-E), even under external force, thereby promoting biorientation between sister k-fibers.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the loss of negative curvature in PRC1 RNAi shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Anchorage along k-fibers is non-uniform and locally reinforced near chromosomes in both the longitudinal and lateral axes.
source: Mapping mechanics over space, microneedle manipulation reveals that anchorage along k-fibers is non-uniform and locally reinforced near chromosomes in both the longitudinal and lateral axes (Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by curvature analysis in Figure 3.

claim: Specialized reinforcement near chromosomes could help protect kinetochore-microtubule attachments and chromosomes from transient forces.
source: In principle, specialized reinforcement near chromosomes could help protect kinetochore-microtubule attachments and chromosomes from transient forces, and ensure that sister k-fibers point to opposite poles (Figure 2E–H) – while allowing them to bend further away and focus into poles.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed reinforcement pattern.

claim: Local anchorage at the spindle center can robustly resist structural changes due to forces over seconds, and yet remodel over minutes.
source: Mapping mechanics over time, our findings indicate that local anchorage at the spindle center can robustly resist structural changes due to forces over seconds (Figure 2F, Figure 3), and yet remodel over minutes.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the 20 s lifetime of reinforcement and comparison to longer timescales.

claim: Spindle structural and functional robustness emerge in part from differentially responding to forces over different timescales.
source: Our findings suggest that spindle structural and functional robustness emerge in part from differentially responding to forces over different timescales.
evidence: This is inferred from the timescale-dependent mechanical response.

claim: The spindle center's remodeling timescale likely reflects the turnover of underlying connections, for example of non-kMTs or of PRC1.
source: While the molecular basis of the spindle center's remodeling timescale is not known, it likely reflects the turnover of underlying connections, for example of non-kMTs (Saxton et al., 1984) or of PRC1 (Pamula et al., 2019; Subramanian et al., 2010), just as crosslinking dynamics contribute to the physical properties of Xenopus extract spindles (Shimamoto et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculated based on known turnover rates from cited studies.

claim: Tuning the lifetime of connections that reinforce the spindle center could regulate its remodeling to allow kinetochores to only sense forces of a given timescale.
source: By tuning the lifetime of these connections that reinforce the spindle center, the cell could in principle regulate its remodeling to allow kinetochores to only sense forces of a given timescale.
evidence: This is speculated as a potential mechanism.

claim: Regulating the timescale of remodeling can enable spindle morphology to change only when needed, for instance at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition.
source: Furthermore, regulating the timescale of remodeling can enable spindle morphology to change only when needed, for instance at the metaphase-to-anaphase transition (Zhu and Jiang, 2005; Zhu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is speculated with support from citations about metaphase-to-anaphase transition.

claim: Mechanical heterogeneity is a principle for how the spindle can be at once dynamic and mechanically robust.
source: Altogether, our work suggests that mechanical heterogeneity is a simple principle for how the spindle and other macromolecular machines can be at once dynamic and mechanically robust.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from all the findings.

claim: Mechanical heterogeneity over space and time allows machines to be reinforced in specific regions and on short timescales for local functions, while allowing remodeling elsewhere and on longer timescales.
source: Mechanical heterogeneity over space and time allows these machines to be reinforced in specific regions and on short timescales for local functions, while allowing remodeling elsewhere and on longer timescales – to ultimately perform robust cellular-scale functions.
evidence: This is a general principle inferred from the findings.

claim: PtK2 GFP-α-tubulin cells were cultured in MEM supplemented with sodium pyruvate, non-essential amino acids, penicillin/streptomycin, and 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum.
source: PtK2 GFP-α-tubulin cells were cultured in MEM (11095; Thermo Fisher, Waltham, MA) supplemented with sodium pyruvate (11360; Thermo Fisher), non-essential amino acids (11140; Thermo Fisher), penicillin/streptomycin, and 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum (10438; Thermo Fisher).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Cells were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO2.
source: Cells were maintained at 37°C and 5% CO2.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: For PRC1 depletion, cells were transfected with siRNA (5'-GGACTGAGGUUGUCAAGAA-3') using Oligofectamine.
source: For depletion of PRC1, cells were transfected with siRNA (5'-GGACTGAGGUUGUCAAGAA-3') for PRC1 using Oligofectamine (Life Technologies, Carlsbad, CA) as previously described (Udy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Cells were imaged 72 hr after siRNA treatment.
source: Cells were imaged 72 hr after siRNA treatment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail.

claim: Western blot analysis showed an 88% decrease of PRC1 levels in PRC1 RNAi vs. mock RNAi conditions.
source: Western blot analysis showed an 88% decrease of PRC1 levels in PRC1 RNAi vs. mock RNAi (Luciferase) conditions, after normalizing to tubulin levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is measured from western blot shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: By immunofluorescence, the average per pixel PRC1 intensity in the spindle above that in the cytoplasm was 597.1 ± 13.7 (AU) in mock RNAi and 145.4 ± 22.3 (AU) in PRC1 RNAi cells (76% knock-down).
source: By immunofluorescence, the average per pixel PRC1 intensity in the spindle above that in the cytoplasm was 597.1 ± 13.7 (AU) (SEM, n = 12) in mock RNAi and 145.4 ± 22.3 (AU) (SEM, n = 24) in PRC1 RNAi cells (76% knock-down, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is measured from immunofluorescence shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: PRC1 knockdown resulted in enrichment of binucleated cells from 4% in mock RNAi to 35% in PRC1 RNAi.
source: We confirmed PRC1 knockdown in the particular coverslips used for live imaging by verifying at low magnification the enrichment of binucleated cells (from 4% (n = 200 cells) in mock RNAi to 35% of cells (n = 213) in PRC1 RNAi) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D), a previously characterized consequence of PRC1 knockdown (Mollinari et al., 2002; Udy et al., 2015).
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.
